segments.translit: /don de nyid lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' bas bskul ba'i yid kyi grub pa'i slob dpon b+hu su ku'i zhabs kyis ri dgas kyi dgongs pa rnam par sgom par byed pa nyid kyis so/
segments.translation: That same meaning is taught by the [siddha]{siddha} master [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku}, whose mind is spurred on by [innate joy]{sahajananda}, through [meditation]{bhavana} on the intent of the [deer]{deer}.
segments.note: Munidatta, in the Tibetan, introduces the song: [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku}, his mind spurred on by [innate joy]{sahajananda}, teaches 'that same meaning' by meditating on the intent (dgongs pa) of the [deer]{deer}, a word Toh 2293 also uses for [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} (cp.23.m1).

flags.note: The Nepal manuscript lacks four leaves here, so Munidatta's comment on song 23 survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293). This segment and the five after it (cp.23.m1 to cp.23.m6) are translations of the Tibetan translation; there is no Sanskrit to compare, and every Sanskrit word named in these flags is inferred through the Tibetan only.

The Tibetan has no finite verb: it ends with two instrumentals, the agent (b+hu su ku'i zhabs kyis) and the means (sgom par byed pa nyid kyis so). 'Is taught' is supplied; the Sanskrit presumably had a verb of speaking ('he says').

ri dgas kyi dgongs pa, 'the intent of the deer': dgongs pa is the Tibetan translators' word for sandhyā in dgongs pa'i skad, 'twilight language', so the Sanskrit may have meant 'the twilight language of the deer' (compare hariṇāśabdasandhyābhāṣayā, cited under the deer entry from song 6). rnam par sgom pa, 'meditating', may render vibhāvanā, which also means 'making clear, setting forth'; then 'setting forth the twilight sense of the deer'. I kept the Tibetan's literal sense.

segments.translit: /gang gi tshe khyod ces bya ba la sogs pa ni kye'i b+hu su ku khyod gal te lus rlung gi ri dgas lus kyi rlung gi ngo bo'o/ /rngon pa zhes pa ni rang bzhin med par byed pa'i thabs tshol bas 'gro bar bya'o/ /de'i tshe yul lnga rnams la gzugs kyi phung por gyur pa me long lta bu'i sa'i khams mig gi dbang po la sogs pa la dkyil 'khor rnams sdud pa'i rim pas gsod pa ni rang bzhin med par byed pa thog mar byed par 'gyur ro/ /slar yang rdo rje'i bzlas pas snang ba gnyis po 'gog cing yang dag par rdo rje dang chu skyes mnyam du sbyor ba bla ma'i drin las bde ba chen po'i 'khor lor chu skyes tshal du rab tu zhugs pa la/ /yid gcig tu byed pa ni rnam par rtog pa med par 'gyur ba rang nyid kyis bdag la yang dag par 'bod par byed pa'o/
segments.translation: 'When you' and so on: 'O [Bhusuku]{p-bhusuku}, if you…'. The [deer]{deer} of body-[wind]{vayu} is the very nature of the [body]{body}'s [wind]{vayu}. '[Hunting]{hunt}' means that one is to set out in search of the [means]{upaya} of making it [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}. Then, to 'kill' the five [sense objects]{visaya}, which have become the [aggregate]{skandha} of form, the [mirror-like wisdom]{adarsajnana}, the earth [element]{dhatu}, the [sense]{indriya} of the eye and so on, by the process of [withdrawal]{upasamhara} of the [maṇḍalas]{mandala}, is first to make them [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}. Next, stopping the two [appearances]{abhasa} by [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}, and rightly joining [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus} together, one enters, by the [guru]{guru}'s [grace]{prasada}, the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}, the [lotus grove]{nalinivana}. There, 'making the mind one' means becoming free of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}: he himself is truly addressing himself.
segments.note: Munidatta, in the Tibetan, makes the quarry the [deer]{deer} of the body's [wind]{vayu}, and [hunting]{hunt} a search for the means of making it without intrinsic nature. Killing the five (in his paraphrase, the five sense objects) by withdrawing the maṇḍalas does that first; vajra recitation and union then lead into the [lotus grove]{nalinivana}, the wheel of great bliss (cp.23.m2).

equations.en: setting out in search of the means of making it without intrinsic nature

equations.src: ལུས་རླུང་གི་རི་དགས lus rlung gi ri dgas
equations.en: the very nature of the body's wind
first making the five sense objects without intrinsic nature, by withdrawing the maṇḍalas

equations.src: ཡིད་གཅིག་ཏུ་བྱེད་པ yid gcig tu byed pa

flags.note: The opening is elliptical: kye'i b+hu su ku khyod gal te ('O Bhusuku, if you') breaks off without a verb, and lus rlung gi ri dgas lus kyi rlung gi ngo bo'o follows. I take the second clause as a separate identification ('the deer of body-wind is the very nature of the body's wind'). It may instead supply the object of the broken-off clause: 'if you [hunt] the deer of body-wind, the nature of the body's wind'. Line 1a has no deer; the comment brings it in.

The lemma has gang gi tshe, 'when', as the Tibetan line does (gang tshe), but the gloss has gal te, 'if', which matches the Bengali jai and the draft's 'If you'. The Sanskrit presumably had yadi, 'if'; this is inferred only through the Tibetan. I kept 'when' in the lemma.

me long lta bu, 'the mirror-like', has no ye shes, 'wisdom'; I supply 'mirror-like wisdom' with the glossary. The list (aggregate of form, mirror-like, earth element, eye faculty) is linked by genitives (me long lta bu'i sa'i khams), apparently the members of one Sanskrit compound; read as 'the earth element of the mirror-like' it makes little sense. sdud pa'i rim pa, 'process of withdrawal', presumably renders (upa)saṃhārakrama; that too is inferred through the Tibetan only.

yid gcig tu byed pa, 'making the mind one', is the glossary's ekamanas (approved 'one-minded'). I left it unmarked: the comment's lemma is causative, following the Tibetan line's imperative (yid ni gcig tu gyis, 'make the mind one'), while the Bengali and the draft have 'you will become one-minded', so the approved surface would misstate the Tibetan wording.

rang nyid kyis bdag la yang dag par 'bod par byed pa, 'he himself is truly addressing himself': yang dag par 'bod pa looks like a calque of Sanskrit sambodhana, 'addressing' (the vocative), which can also be heard as 'awakening'; so possibly 'he himself fully awakens himself'. The clause can also be parsed 'he himself, having become free of conceptual thought, addresses himself', which explains why the song speaks to Bhusuku in the second person rather than glossing 'one mind'. I chose the first parse, which matches the glossary's reading of ekamanas.

The comment's word for the lotus grove is chu skyes tshal, where the Tibetan line has pad+ma'i tshal. chu skyes, 'water-born', fits a Sanskrit like nalinī- or jalaja- and the Bengali nalaṇībana better, a hint that the commentary's lemma was not taken from the Tibetan song text.

segments.translit: /de'i phyir d+h+rU'i rkang pas brtan pa la dmigs pa gsal por byed pa gsungs te/ gson po zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni rab tu zhugs pa'i dbugs ni gson po la oM yig nyin mo'i shes pas rang bzhin bzhi bcu'i rang bzhin dang ldan pa'o/ /dbyung ba'i dbugs shi ba'i ro hUM yig mtshan mo'i shes pa'i rang bzhin sum cu rtsa gsum gyi rang bzhin gyi ngo bo'o/ /gnas pa'i dbugs kyi bzhi AH yig ma ning gi shes pa'i rang bzhin bdun gyi rang bzhin dang ldan pa'o/ /de bzhin du phyag na rdo rjes kyang / oM yig gis 'jug sems can rnams/ /sangs rgyas sku nyid mchog tu rtag /hUM yig 'byin byed sems can rnams/ /AH yig gis ni gnas par byed/ /de bzhin du snang ba mtshan mo'i cha nyid kyis zhes bya ba la sogs pa rgya cher gsungs so/ /dang por srog la sogs pa'i shes pa dbu mar rab tu zhugs par byas nas de'i rjes su sha ni dgongs pa'i skad kyi khyad par gyi dga' ba rang byin gyis brlab pa'i ngo bo nyid bzhi pa'i dga' pas ma sbyangs na kye'i b+hu su ku'i zhabs bde ba chen po'i khyim du 'jug par mi byed pa'o/ /de bzhin du rim pa lnga las kyang / mtshan mo ma yin mtshams kyang min/ /nyin mo yang ni ma yin no/ /zhes bya ba la sogs pa gsungs so/ /de bzhin du sa ra ha'i zhabs kyis kyang / dbang po gang du nub cing mi gnas rang bzhin la/ /kye'i lhan cig skyes dga' bla ma'i zhabs la dris/
segments.translation: Therefore, with the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he teaches how to make clear the focus on what is steady. 'The [living]{jivanta}' and so on: the entering [breath]{breath} is the living; it is the syllable oṃ, and through the knowledge of day it has the nature of the forty [natures]{prakrti}. The outgoing [breath]{breath} is 'the corpse of the [dead]{mrta}': it is the syllable hūṃ, the knowledge of [night]{night}, whose nature is that of the thirty-three [natures]{prakrti}. The abiding [breath]{breath} is the syllable āḥ, the knowledge of the [neuter]{napumsaka}, and it has the nature of the seven [natures]{prakrti}. So [Vajrapāṇi]{p-vajrapani} too says: 'By the syllable oṃ beings enter: / the [buddha]{buddha} body itself, supreme and constant. / The syllable hūṃ makes beings go out; / by the syllable āḥ they are made to abide.' Likewise it is taught at length: '[Light]{aloka}, by its very share of [night]{night}…' and so on. First the knowledges of the life-force and the rest are made to enter the [central channel]{madhyama}; after that, '[flesh]{mamsa}' is, in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, whose nature is [self-blessing]{svadhisthana}: unless it is purified by the fourth [joy]{ananda}, O [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku}, you do not enter the [house]{house} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}. So too the [Five Stages]{pancakrama} says: 'It is not night, nor is it twilight; / nor is it day,' and so on. So too [Saraha]{p-saraha} says: 'Of that nature in which the [senses]{indriya} sink and do not stay, / of [innate joy]{sahajananda}, O, ask at the [guru]{guru}'s feet.'
segments.note: Munidatta, in the Tibetan, reads the refrain through the breath: the living is the entering [breath]{breath} (oṃ, knowledge of day, forty natures), the dead the outgoing (hūṃ, night, thirty-three); an abiding breath goes with āḥ. [Flesh]{mamsa} is twilight language for the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}: unless the fourth joy purifies it, one does not enter the house of great bliss (cp.23.m3).

equations.en: in twilight language, the joy of cessation, whose nature is self-blessing

citations.quoted: By the syllable oṃ beings enter: / the buddha body itself, supreme and constant. / The syllable hūṃ makes beings go out; / by the syllable āḥ they are made to abide.
citations.work: attributed to Vajrapāṇi (phyag na rdo rje); no work is named, and which Vajrapāṇi is meant is not said

citations.quoted: Light, by its very share of night…
citations.work: unnamed; cited as taught 'at length' right after the Vajrapāṇi verse, perhaps from the same source or from a Guhyasamāja completion-stage text

citations.quoted: It is not night, nor is it twilight; / nor is it day…
citations.work: Pañcakrama (named as rim pa lnga, 'the Five Stages')

citations.quoted: Of that nature in which the senses sink and do not stay, / of innate joy, O, ask at the guru's feet.
citations.work: Saraha (named as sa ra ha'i zhabs); no work is named, presumably one of his dohās

flags.note: d+h+rU'i rkang pas brtan pa la dmigs pa gsal por byed pa: brtan pa, 'steady', is the Tibetan for dhruva, the same word as in dhruvapada, 'refrain' (the Tibetan elsewhere calls the refrain brtan pa'i rkang pa). So this may be a gloss on the refrain's name ('with the dhru verse, the steady one, he teaches making the focus clear') or a pun on dhruva ('the focus on what is steady'). I chose the second, which keeps the Tibetan grammar.
gnas pa'i dbugs kyi bzhi, literally 'the four of the abiding breath', makes no sense; bzhi may be a slip for gzhi, 'basis', or for bzhin. I left it untranslated ('The abiding breath is…').

In the unnamed quotation, snang ba could render āloka, 'light', or ābhāsa, 'appearance'. I chose 'light' because the passage is built on the Guhyasamāja scheme of three lights with forty, thirty-three and seven natures, and on the tie of day, night and the neuter to them; the Sanskrit can be inferred only through the Tibetan.

The comment's 'house of great bliss' (bde ba chen po'i khyim) follows the Tibetan line 2b (khyim du 'jug ma byed, 'do not enter the house'), where the Bengali has padmabaṇa and the draft 'lotus grove'. The comment and the Tibetan line agree against the Bengali, so this was probably the reading of the manuscript the translators used.

Inferred only through the Tibetan: khyad par gyi dga' ba is taken as viramānanda, 'joy of cessation', following the glossary's evidence from other songs of Toh 2293; srog, 'life-force', presumably renders prāṇa; shes pa is rendered 'knowledge' throughout, so 'the knowledges of the life-force and the rest' echoes the knowledges of day, night and the neuter.

dga' pas (bzhi pa'i dga' pas ma sbyangs na) is evidently a slip for dga' bas, 'by the joy'; the transliteration keeps what is written. AHyig in the machine Wylie is written AH yig. The segment ends with Saraha's couplet without a closing zhes gsungs so, so the quotation may be cut short.

segments.translit: /rkang pa gnyis pas lam gyi thabs gsungs te/ sgyu 'phrul dra ba zhes bya ba la sogs pa'i sgyu ma zhes pa ni las kyi yan lag tu rtogs par bya ste/ rnam pa sna tshogs pa la sogs pa'i skad cig la thob pa de'i bde ba la tshogs pa'i lus la dra ba gzhag pa ste/ de yis lus kyi ri dgas 'ching bar byed pa bla ma'i zhabs kyi drin las de'i ngo bo khong du chud par bya'o/ /de'i phyir de la bde ba nyams su myong ba'i ngo bo nyid thob pa de'i tshe gang du yang brjod par mi nus pa'o/ /de bzhin du sa ra ha'i zhabs kyis kyang / dga' bas mnyes gshin 'jig rten zhes bya ba la sogs pa gsungs so/
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he teaches the [means]{upaya} of the [path]{marga}. 'The [net of illusion]{mayajala}' and so on: '[illusion]{maya}' is to be understood as the limb of action. In the [bliss]{sukha} gained in the moments beginning with [vicitra]{vicitra}, the net is laid on the assembled body; with it the [deer]{deer} of the [body]{body} is bound, and by the [grace]{prasada} of the [guru]{guru}'s feet one is to realize its nature. So when one has gained there the nature of the experience of [bliss]{sukha}, at that time it cannot be told anywhere at all. So too [Saraha]{p-saraha} says: 'Pleased with [joy]{ananda}, gentle, the world…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta, in the Tibetan, takes this couplet as the means of the path. 'Illusion' is the 'limb of action', probably the action woman (karmamudrā). In the bliss of the moments beginning with [vicitra]{vicitra} ('variety', the first moment) a net is laid on the body and binds the [deer]{deer} of the body; that bliss, once experienced, cannot be told (cp.23.m4).

equations.en: the limb of action (las kyi yan lag), probably for karmāṅganā, 'action woman', the karmamudrā

citations.quoted: Pleased with joy, gentle, the world…
citations.work: Saraha (named as sa ra ha'i zhabs); no work is named

flags.note: las kyi yan lag, literally 'limb of action'. The glossary records las kyi yan lag elsewhere in Toh 2293 for karmāṅganā, 'action woman', a name of the karmamudrā; the translators apparently read aṅganā, 'woman', as aṅga, 'limb'. So the Sanskrit probably said 'illusion is the action woman'. That is inferred only through the Tibetan. I translated the Tibetan literally and did not mark it {karmamudra}.

The lemma is sgyu 'phrul dra ba, 'net of illusion', but the word glossed is sgyu ma, the form in the Tibetan line's sgyu ma'i ri dgas, 'illusory deer'. So 'illusion' may be the illusion of the net or of the doe; the comment does not say which.

de'i bde ba la tshogs pa'i lus la dra ba gzhag pa: I read 'in that bliss, the net is laid on the assembled body' (tshogs pa'i lus as the body as a composite). It can also be read 'on the body gathered in that bliss'.

The comment has the deer bound ('ching bar byed pa), agreeing with the Bengali bādheli, 'bound', against the Tibetan line 3a, which has gsad par gyis, 'kill'. So the commentary's text of the song read 'bind' here.

Saraha's quotation, dga' bas mnyes gshin 'jig rten, is too short to construe: gshin can mean 'gentle, kind' or 'the dead', and mnyes gshin might be a slip for mnyen gshin, 'soft'. My English is a word-by-word guess.

segments.translit: /rkang pa gsum pas goms pa'i khyad par du gsungs so/ /lus snod ces bya ba la sogs pa'i lus nyid ni bdag gi snod gzhir gyur pa de las 'byung ba chen po lngar gyur pa'i rdzas bza' bar bya'o/ /de la dus dang dus min ni zla ba nyi ma dag dang gsum pa a wa d+hU tI'i rlung la bzhi pa'i dga' bas thams cad yongs su 'joms pa'i phyir/ bza' ba dang btung ba ni rang bzhin med par byed pa'o/ /de bzhin du dpal dus kyi 'khor lo las kyang / gang zhig thig le dkar 'dzin lhung na nyin mtshan zhes bya ba la sogs pa gsungs so/
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he teaches what is special in [practice]{abhyasa}. 'The [body]{body}, the [vessel]{vessel}' and so on: the [body]{body} itself has become my [vessel]{vessel} and base, and from it one is to eat the substances that have become the five [great elements]{mahabhuta}. There, '[time and non-time]{time-non-time}' are the [moon]{moon} and the [sun]{surya}, and the third is the [wind]{vayu} of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}; because the fourth [joy]{ananda} utterly destroys them all, 'eating and drinking' is making them [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}. So too the glorious [Kālacakra]{tx-kalacakra} says: 'Whoever holds the white [drop]{bindu}, if it falls, day and night…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta, in the Tibetan, takes this couplet as practice in its special character: from the body-vessel one eats substances become the five [great elements]{mahabhuta}. [Time and non-time]{time-non-time} are the moon and sun, with the wind of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} (central channel) third; the fourth joy destroys them all, so eating and drinking is making them without intrinsic nature (cp.23.m5).

equations.en: the moon and the sun, with the wind of the avadhūtī as a third

equations.src: བཟའ་བ་དང་བཏུང་བ bza' ba dang btung ba

citations.quoted: Whoever holds the white drop, if it falls, day and night…
citations.work: Kālacakra (named as dpal dus kyi 'khor lo, 'the glorious Kālacakra'); which text of the cycle is not said

flags.note: The comment explains 'eating and drinking' (bza' ba dang btung ba), but the Tibetan text of couplet 4 has only zas, 'food' (4a), and no drinking. The commentary's text of the song may have differed here, or the phrase paraphrases the line.

goms pa'i khyad par, 'what is special in practice': goms pa regularly renders abhyāsa (see the glossary entry), so the Sanskrit was perhaps abhyāsaviśeṣa; khyad par might also mean 'a particular kind of practice'. Inferred only through the Tibetan.

The Kālacakra quotation (gang zhig thig le dkar 'dzin lhung na nyin mtshan) is a fragment: dkar 'dzin may be 'holds the white [drop]' or part of a name, and nyin mtshan, 'day and night', has no construction. My English is tentative.
bdag gi snod gzhir gyur pa: bdag gi may be 'my', as in the line and the draft ('my vessel'), or 'of oneself, of the self'. I kept 'my' for consistency with the draft.

segments.translit: /rkang pa bzhi pas 'bras bu rdzogs pa gsungs te/ rgya dang rdos zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni de la bde ba chen po'i dga' ba ni rgya zhes te dgongs pa'i skad kyi sku'i dga' ba'i rnam par rtog pa'o/ /rdos zhes bya ba ni dgongs pa'i skad kyis gsung gi dga' ba'i rnam par rtog pa'o/ /thag pa zhes pa ni thugs kyi dga' ba'i rnam par rtog pa'o/ /de rnams thams cad gzugs la sogs pa yang nam mkha'o/ /brgyug pa zhes pa ni 'od gsal 'bebs pa de nyid rlung gi ngo bo lus kyi ri dgas so/ /bros pa ni rang bzhin med par gyur pa rtag tu goms pa'i rnal 'byor pas nam mkhar 'od gsal la thim par gyur pa'o/ /de'i phyir b+hu su ku'i zhabs kyis mtshan mo zhes pa ni ma rig pa'i mun pa sangs pa ni bros pa zhes pa'i don to/ /de bzhin du lung las kyang / bdag nyid de bzhin thig gyur te/ /bcom ldan 'das ni srog gi bdag /ces bya ba la sogs pa gsungs so/
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he teaches the completion of the fruit. '[Net]{net} and [stone]{stone}' and so on: here, as for the [joy]{ananda} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, '[net]{net}' is, in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} about the [joy]{ananda} of body. '[Stone]{stone}' is, in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} about the [joy]{ananda} of speech. '[Rope]{rope}' is [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} about the [joy]{ananda} of mind. All of these, form and the rest too, are [sky]{gagana}. 'Running': that which descends into [clear light]{prabhasvara} is the [deer]{deer} of the [body]{body}, whose nature is [wind]{vayu}. 'Fled' means that, having become [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}, it has dissolved, through the [yogi]{yogi} of constant [practice]{abhyasa}, into [clear light]{prabhasvara} in the [sky]{gagana}. So in [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku}'s '[night]{night}', the clearing away of the darkness of [ignorance]{avidya} is the meaning of 'fled'. So too the [scripture]{agama} says: 'Oneself likewise becomes a drop; / the [Blessed One]{p-bhagavat} is the lord of life,' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta, in the Tibetan, takes this couplet as the completed fruit. [Net]{net}, [stone]{stone} and [rope]{rope} are twilight language for conceptual thought about the joys of body, speech and mind; all these, form and the rest, are sky. The running [deer]{deer} is the body's wind; its flight is dissolving into clear light, and the clearing of the night, ignorance's darkness (cp.23.m6).

equations.en: conceptual thought about the joy of body
conceptual thought about the joy of speech
conceptual thought about the joy of mind
all of these, form and the rest
the deer of the body, whose nature is wind, descending into clear light
having become without intrinsic nature, dissolving into clear light in the sky
the darkness of ignorance, whose clearing is the sense of 'fled'

citations.quoted: Oneself likewise becomes a drop; / the Blessed One is the lord of life.
citations.work: an unnamed scripture (lung, presumably Sanskrit āgama)

flags.note: de la bde ba chen po'i dga' ba ni rgya zhes te: 'the joy of great bliss' is loosely attached. I read it as a topic ('as for the joy of great bliss'), perhaps for a Sanskrit locative ('in the joy of great bliss'), or as introducing the three joys that follow. Read as 'the joy of great bliss is called net', it would contradict the rest of the gloss.

The Tibetan line 5a has rdo lcags, 'stone [and] iron'; the comment cites only rdos and leaves lcags unexplained, so its three items (net, stone, rope) map onto body, speech and mind. rdo lcags may be one device rather than two.

'od gsal 'bebs pa: 'bebs pa is transitive ('bring down, cast'), so the phrase may mean 'that which brings down clear light' rather than 'that which descends into clear light'. I chose the latter, which fits the deer's dissolving into clear light in the next sentence.

de'i phyir b+hu su ku'i zhabs kyis mtshan mo zhes pa ni ma rig pa'i mun pa sangs pa ni bros pa zhes pa'i don to has two topics. I translated it as it stands; it may stand for 'night is the darkness of ignorance; its clearing is what fled means', joining 5a's flight to 6a's dawn. This sentence is the only comment on line 6a.

In the scripture quotation, thig gyur may mean 'became a drop' (thig, as in thig le or thig pa) or be a slip for thim gyur, 'dissolved', which the preceding sentence uses (thim par gyur pa). I translated 'becomes a drop' and left it unmarked; with thim the line would read 'Oneself likewise dissolves'.

proposals.definition: The neuter (Sanskrit napuṃsaka, Tibetan ma ning): neither male nor female. Munidatta, in the Tibetan, joins the abiding breath and the syllable āḥ to 'the knowledge of the neuter' and seven natures, beside the knowledges of day and night (cp.23.m3); the glossary also records his reading of song 14's pulinda as 'the neuter' (cp.14.m5).
proposals.rationale: The word recurs in Munidatta's schemes of breath and light (cp.14.m5, cp.23.m3) and is easily taken as grammatical gender; an entry keeps 'neuter' consistent.

questions: cp.23.m4: should las kyi yan lag stay literal ('limb of action'), or be rendered as the karmamudrā it probably stands for (karmāṅganā, 'action woman'), marked [karmamudrā]{karmamudra}?

cp.23.m2: yid gcig tu byed pa ('making the mind one') is left unmarked although it is the glossary's ekamanas, because the Tibetan lemma is causative and 'one-minded' would misstate it. Mark it anyway, or add 'making the mind one' as a variant for the Tibetan comment?

cp.23.m3: the comment, like the Tibetan line, has 'the house (khyim) of great bliss' where the Bengali 2b has padmabaṇa and the draft 'lotus grove'. Should the draft's note on 2b record that Munidatta's comment (cp.23.m3) agrees with the Tibetan line?
cp.23.m4: the comment's 'binds' agrees with the Bengali bādheli against the Tibetan line's 'kill' (gsad par gyis). Worth a witness note on 3a?
cp.23.m3: I rendered snang ba in the unnamed quotation as 'light' (āloka) rather than 'appearance' (ābhāsa), because of the forty, thirty-three and seven natures. Agree?
cp.23.m2: the lemma 'When you' keeps the Tibetan gang gi tshe, while the draft's 1a has 'If you' (the gloss itself has gal te, 'if'). Keep the lemma literal, or align it with the draft?
Proposal napumsaka ('neuter'): adopt, or fold into an existing entry?
